title: Moving Abroad With a Family: Schools, Visas, and Spousal Work for International Teachers
excerpt: The three questions every teacher with a family has to answer before signing an international contract: whose visa covers whom, where the kids go to school, and whether your partner can work.
content:
Moving Abroad With a Family: Schools, Visas, and Spousal Work for International Teachers

Moving abroad on your own is a logistics puzzle. Moving abroad with a partner and kids is three puzzles stacked on top of each other, and the pieces don't always fit together the way the recruiter's brochure suggests. Before you sign, you need honest answers to three separate questions: whose visa covers whom, where the children go to school (and who pays for it), and whether your partner can actually work in the country you're moving to.

The recruiter can help you with the first, the school with the second, and almost nobody wants to touch the third. That's the one that ends contracts early.

Key Takeaways

  • About half of international schools cover flights and visa fees for dependents. The other half don't, and you find out which is which by reading the contract, not the brochure [1].
  • Free or heavily subsidised tuition for dependents at tier-1 international schools can be worth $30,000 to $60,000 per child per year [2]. Partial subsidies (25 to 75 percent, or waived registration and exam fees) are more common than full waivers.
  • Spousal work rules vary sharply. Singapore closed the Letter of Consent route for new Dependant's Pass holders in May 2021, so your partner needs their own Employment Pass to work as an employee [3]. Vietnam's TT visa lets a family stay but doesn't grant work rights on its own [4].
  • UAE reforms in 2026 raised the dependent visa sponsor salary floor to AED 4,000 per month and now require the sponsor to hold the family health insurance policy [5].
  • Shipping a 2-3 bedroom household to Asia typically costs $8,000 to $18,000 by 20-foot container [6]. Most experienced international families ship less than they think they will.

Whose visa covers whom, and what it actually costs

The first thing to check is whether the school's relocation package includes your family or only you. Half of schools cover flights and visa application fees for dependents; half don't [1]. Generous packages include a shipping container, visa coverage for the whole family, and short-term housing on arrival. Partial packages might cover the teacher's visa plus a small allowance for the family. Some cover visas only.

The word to look for in the contract is "dependents," not "family." If the offer says "visa sponsorship" without specifying, ask directly whose visa is included and who pays the renewal fee each year. Visa renewals for a family of four add up over a three-year contract.

Documentation is where the small mistakes get expensive. Apostilled marriage and birth certificates are non-negotiable in most jurisdictions, and getting them from your home country after you've already moved is slow and costly. If the name on your work visa doesn't exactly match the name on your shipping manifest or your child's school enrolment, both can be held up for weeks [6]. Double-check every document uses the same spelling and middle-name convention before you leave.

A note on the Middle East before moving on: the UAE's 2026 amendments raised the dependent visa sponsor salary floor to AED 4,000 per month, and applications are now being rejected where only the dependent holds health insurance rather than the sponsor [5]. Family sponsorship rules there are no longer tied to gender or profession, which is a change from earlier years. If your offer is in the Gulf, verify the current salary threshold in writing with the school's HR before signing.

The tuition question: what waivers really cover

Tuition remission for teacher's children is often the single most valuable line in an international school contract, and it's also one of the most inconsistently defined. Full waivers can be worth $30,000 to $60,000 per child per year at tier-1 schools; partial subsidies of 25 to 75 percent, waived registration and exam fees, or a fixed dependent education stipend are more common than a full free ride [2].

What to ask before you sign:

QuestionWhy it matters
How many children does the waiver cover?Some schools cap at two
Does it cover tuition only, or fees too?Registration, exam, activity, and technology fees can add $2,000 to $5,000 per child
Is there a sibling discount if the waiver doesn't stretch?Common sibling discounts run 10 to 25 percent for second and third children [2]
What happens if you leave mid-contract?Some schools claw back tuition for the year in progress
Is your child guaranteed a seat, or is it space-available?Popular schools with long waitlists sometimes hedge this

If your children are younger than the school's minimum enrolment age (many international schools start at age 3 or 4, but some at 5 or 6), the waiver doesn't help you yet, and preschool fees in Bangkok, Ho Chi Minh City, or Singapore can run $8,000 to $15,000 a year out of pocket. Ask what the school's usual handling is for teacher children below enrolment age.

If your children are older than the school offers (some primaries stop at grade 5), you'll need a secondary school that accepts them, and that school's fees are on you unless the contract explicitly says otherwise.

Where the kids actually go to school

Getting the seat is separate from paying for it. Popular international schools in Singapore, Bangkok, and the top-tier schools in Vietnam and China have waitlists that predate your job offer. If the recruiter says "your kids will get in," the follow-up question is: get in when. September of next year isn't the same as September this year.

A few things worth knowing:

  • If both parents teach at the same school, the family is often prioritised in enrolment queues, which can matter more than the waiver itself.
  • Younger siblings usually get sibling priority once one child is enrolled, so the older child's admission is the harder gate.
  • Some schools require a formal admissions process for teacher children (assessment, interview, English proficiency check), which can feel odd when your child is the whole reason you took the job.
  • Grade placement across curricula isn't always one-to-one. A US 4th-grader landing in a British-curriculum Year 5 (or vice versa) may sit half a year ahead or behind their age peers depending on cutoff dates. Ask the receiving school before you leave what year your child will actually be placed in.

If your family has a child with additional learning needs, ask specifically what SEN or learning support the school provides and what the wait for assessment looks like. Support levels vary, and a school that says "we accommodate all learners" in the brochure sometimes has one part-time specialist for a school of 900.

The trailing spouse problem: can your partner work

This is the topic that recruiters skirt around. Whether your partner can legally work in your new country is a function of visa type, salary threshold, and paperwork, and the answer differs sharply from country to country.

Singapore. Most spouses hold a Dependant's Pass (DP), which allows residence but not employment. The Letter of Consent (LOC) that used to let DP holders work for a Singapore employer was closed to new DP-holder employees in May 2021 [3]. If your partner wants to work as an employee, they need their own Employment Pass, S Pass, or Work Permit through a sponsoring employer. The narrow remaining LOC exception is for DP holders who want to establish or operate their own business, and even then they generally need to hold at least 30 percent shareholding [3]. From 1 July 2026, the Local Qualifying Salary also rose from S$1,600 to S$1,800 per month, which affects DP-business-owner LOCs coming up for renewal in the second half of 2026 [3].

Vietnam. A partner enters on a TT dependent visa, valid up to 12 months, or a residence card on top of that valid up to three years [4]. The TT visa lets the family live in Vietnam but does not authorise employment. To work, your partner needs their own work permit (or a qualifying exemption) plus the matching visa. One recent change: partners married to Vietnamese citizens are exempt from work permits under Decree 219/2025 (effective 7 August 2025), though the employer still has to notify the Department of Home Affairs at least three working days before the start date [4]. That exemption doesn't apply to foreign-foreign couples.

Thailand. A spouse enters on an "O" dependent visa attached to the teacher's Non-Immigrant B. To work, the spouse needs their own work permit sponsored by a Thai employer, which typically requires the employer to meet minimum capitalisation and Thai-to-foreign staff ratio requirements. Remote work for a non-Thai employer sits in a grey area that Thailand has been changing rules around, and the current answer is worth verifying with a Thai immigration lawyer rather than a Facebook post.

UAE. A spouse can work while holding a dependent visa, but a spouse visa does not automatically grant work permission. A separate MOHRE work permit from the new employer is required, along with a no-objection certificate (NOC) from the sponsor [5].

China. Family members can accompany a Z-visa (work) holder on an S1 or S2 dependent visa. The dependent visa itself doesn't grant work rights; the spouse needs their own Z visa via a Chinese employer.

The pattern across all of these: "your family can come with you" is usually true. "Your partner can just get a job when they arrive" almost never is. Plan for six to eighteen months of your partner either not working, working remotely for a home-country employer (with all the tax complications that adds), or hunting for a locally-sponsored role, which is harder in some markets than others.

What to do before you sign

A short checklist, in the order the questions tend to bite:

1. Get the dependent visa policy in writing. Who is covered, who pays application and renewal fees, whose name the sponsor has to be in.

2. Get the tuition waiver policy in writing. Number of children covered, fees included, mid-contract clawback rules, and whether it applies from year one.

3. Confirm actual school placement for each child, not "we'll help you get in." Assessment date, grade placement, waitlist status.

4. Confirm your partner's work rights independently. Talk to an immigration lawyer in the destination country, not just the school's HR.

5. Confirm relocation coverage: shipping (LCL vs full container), temporary housing on arrival, flight allowance for dependents.

6. Confirm health insurance covers the whole family from day one, not just the teacher. Home-country policies rarely cover you abroad [7].

7. Apostille everything (marriage certificate, birth certificates, degrees) before you leave your home country. Getting apostilles remotely is painful.

The families who move abroad and stay past their first contract almost always did the paperwork slower and asked more questions before signing than the ones who leave early. The recruiter is not your enemy, but the recruiter is also not the person who has to live in the answers.
